claim: Cohesin entraps individual DNAs within its SMC-kleisin ring during G1.
source: In addition to extruding DNA loops, cohesin entraps within its SMC-kleisin ring (S-K) individual DNAs during G1 and sister DNAs during S-phase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of cohesin.

claim: Cohesin entraps sister DNAs within its SMC-kleisin ring during S-phase.
source: In addition to extruding DNA loops, cohesin entraps within its SMC-kleisin ring (S-K) individual DNAs during G1 and sister DNAs during S-phase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of cohesin.

claim: All three cohesin activities (loop extrusion, G1 entrapment, S-phase entrapment) require Scc2 and Scc3.
source: All three activities require related hook-shaped proteins called Scc2 and Scc3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Scc2 alone promotes entrapment of DNAs in the E-S compartment.
source: Scc2 alone promotes entrapment of DNAs in the E-S and E-K compartments, between ATP-bound engaged heads and the SMC hinge and associated kleisin, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Scc2 alone promotes entrapment of DNAs in the E-K compartment.
source: Scc2 alone promotes entrapment of DNAs in the E-S and E-K compartments, between ATP-bound engaged heads and the SMC hinge and associated kleisin, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: E-S/E-K entrapment by Scc2 does not require ATP hydrolysis.
source: This does not require ATP hydrolysis nor is it accompanied by entrapment within S-K rings, which is a slower process requiring Scc3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: E-S/E-K entrapment by Scc2 is not accompanied by entrapment within S-K rings.
source: This does not require ATP hydrolysis nor is it accompanied by entrapment within S-K rings, which is a slower process requiring Scc3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: S-K entrapment is a slower process than E-S/E-K entrapment.
source: This does not require ATP hydrolysis nor is it accompanied by entrapment within S-K rings, which is a slower process requiring Scc3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: S-K entrapment requires Scc3.
source: This does not require ATP hydrolysis nor is it accompanied by entrapment within S-K rings, which is a slower process requiring Scc3.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: DNAs transported into E-S/E-K compartments are 'clamped' in a sub-compartment created by Scc2's association with engaged heads.
source: Cryo-EM reveals that DNAs transported into E-S/E-K compartments are 'clamped' in a sub-compartment created by Scc2's association with engaged heads whose coiled coils are folded around their elbow.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The coiled coils of engaged heads are folded around their elbow during DNA clamping.
source: Cryo-EM reveals that DNAs transported into E-S/E-K compartments are 'clamped' in a sub-compartment created by Scc2's association with engaged heads whose coiled coils are folded around their elbow.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Clamping may be a recurrent feature of cohesin complexes active in loop extrusion.
source: We suggest that clamping may be a recurrent feature of cohesin complexes active in loop extrusion and that this conformation precedes the S-K entrapment required for sister chromatid cohesion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a suggestion based on the findings.

claim: The clamped conformation precedes S-K entrapment required for sister chromatid cohesion.
source: We suggest that clamping may be a recurrent feature of cohesin complexes active in loop extrusion and that this conformation precedes the S-K entrapment required for sister chromatid cohesion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a suggestion based on the findings.

claim: Cohesin mediates connections between sister DNAs that hold sister chromatids together during mitosis.
source: Cohesin in addition mediates the connections between sister DNAs that hold sister chromatids together during mitosis until their disjunction at the onset of anaphase (Oliveira et al., 2010; Uhlmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: SMC proteins contain a dimerisation domain (hinge) at one end and an ABC-like ATPase domain at the other end.
source: All contain a pair of rod-shaped SMC proteins with a dimerisation domain, known as the hinge, at one end and an ABC-like ATPase domain at the other, separated by a ~ 50 nm long anti-parallel intra-molecular coiled coil (Haering et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the structural description.

claim: The hinge and ATPase domains of SMC proteins are separated by a ~50 nm long anti-parallel intra-molecular coiled coil.
source: All contain a pair of rod-shaped SMC proteins with a dimerisation domain, known as the hinge, at one end and an ABC-like ATPase domain at the other, separated by a ~ 50 nm long anti-parallel intra-molecular coiled coil (Haering et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the structural description.

claim: Scc1's N-terminal domain forms a three-helix bundle with the coiled coil emerging from Smc3's ATPase head.
source: Their association creates V-shaped dimers whose apical ATPase head domains are interconnected by a kleisin subunit (Scc1) whose N-terminal domain forms a three-helix bundle with the coiled coil emerging from Smc3's ATPase head (Gligoris et al., 2014), called its neck, and whose C-terminal winged helical domain binds to the base (or cap) of Smc1's ATPase head to complete the ring (Haering et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the structural description.

claim: Scc1's C-terminal winged helical domain binds to the base of Smc1's ATPase head to complete the ring.
source: Their association creates V-shaped dimers whose apical ATPase head domains are interconnected by a kleisin subunit (Scc1) whose N-terminal domain forms a three-helix bundle with the coiled coil emerging from Smc3's ATPase head (Gligoris et al., 2014), called its neck, and whose C-terminal winged helical domain binds to the base (or cap) of Smc1's ATPase head to complete the ring (Haering et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the structural description.

claim: Hinge dimerisation facilitates extensive contacts between Smc1 and Smc3 coiled coils.
source: Hinge dimerisation facilitates numerous other contacts between Smc1 and Smc3. First, their coiled coils interact with each other extensively, all the way from the hinge to the joint, a small break in the coiled coil roughly 5 nm above the heads, effectively zipping up the coiled coils (Bürmann et al., 2019; Chapard et al., 2019; Diebold-Durand et al., 2017; Soh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the structural description.

claim: The coiled coils of Smc1 and Smc3 fold around an elbow, resulting in interaction between the hinge and a section of the coiled coils approximately 10 nm from the heads.
source: Second, their coiled coils fold around an elbow, which results in an interaction between the hinge and a section of the coiled coils approximately 10 nm from the heads (Bürmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the structural description.

claim: Head engagement involves the γ-phosphate of ATP bound to one ATPase head binding a signature motif on the other head.
source: Finally, the γ-phosphate of ATP bound to one ATPase head binds a signature motif on the other, resulting under appropriate conditions in engagement of the heads and a sandwiching of two molecules of ATP between them, a process that is a precondition for subsequent ATP hydrolysis (Arumugam et al., 2003; Lammens et al., 2004; Íñigo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the mechanism.

claim: Head engagement is a precondition for ATP hydrolysis.
source: Finally, the γ-phosphate of ATP bound to one ATPase head binds a signature motif on the other, resulting under appropriate conditions in engagement of the heads and a sandwiching of two molecules of ATP between them, a process that is a precondition for subsequent ATP hydrolysis (Arumugam et al., 2003; Lammens et al., 2004; Íñigo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the mechanism.

claim: Scc2 is essential for cohesin's ATPase activity.
source: Scc2 is essential for cohesin's ATPase activity (Petela et al., 2018), for its loading onto chromosomes (Ciosk et al., 2000), for maintaining cohesin's chromosomal association during G1 (Srinivasan et al., 2019), and for cohesin's ability to extrude loops in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Scc2 is essential for cohesin loading onto chromosomes.
source: Scc2 is essential for cohesin's ATPase activity (Petela et al., 2018), for its loading onto chromosomes (Ciosk et al., 2000), for maintaining cohesin's chromosomal association during G1 (Srinivasan et al., 2019), and for cohesin's ability to extrude loops in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Scc2 is essential for maintaining cohesin's chromosomal association during G1.
source: Scc2 is essential for cohesin's ATPase activity (Petela et al., 2018), for its loading onto chromosomes (Ciosk et al., 2000), for maintaining cohesin's chromosomal association during G1 (Srinivasan et al., 2019), and for cohesin's ability to extrude loops in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Scc2 is essential for cohesin's ability to extrude loops in vitro.
source: Scc2 is essential for cohesin's ATPase activity (Petela et al., 2018), for its loading onto chromosomes (Ciosk et al., 2000), for maintaining cohesin's chromosomal association during G1 (Srinivasan et al., 2019), and for cohesin's ability to extrude loops in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Scc2 is not required to maintain cohesion during G2.
source: However, Scc2 is not required to maintain cohesion during G2 or even establish cohesion during S phase from complexes previously associated with unreplicated DNAs (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Around 20% of cohesin complexes can be crosslinked simultaneously at all three interfaces in vivo.
source: Around 20% of cohesin complexes can be crosslinked simultaneously at all three interfaces in vivo (Gligoris et al., 2014), and in post-replicative cells this is accompanied by formation of SDS-resistant structures that hold together the sister DNAs of circular minichromosomes, called catenated dimers or CDs (Chapard et al., 2019; Gligoris et al., 2014; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In post-replicative cells, crosslinking at all three interfaces is accompanied by formation of catenated dimers (CDs).
source: Around 20% of cohesin complexes can be crosslinked simultaneously at all three interfaces in vivo (Gligoris et al., 2014), and in post-replicative cells this is accompanied by formation of SDS-resistant structures that hold together the sister DNAs of circular minichromosomes, called catenated dimers or CDs (Chapard et al., 2019; Gligoris et al., 2014; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: There is a perfect correlation between CD formation and cohesion establishment.
source: Importantly, the study of numerous mutants has revealed a perfect correlation between CD formation and cohesion establishment (Srinivasan et al., 2018), suggesting that these structures are actually responsible for sister chromatid cohesion or at the very least are produced by a highly related mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Sister DNAs are entrapped between juxtaposed heads and the kleisin associated with them (J-K compartment).
source: Using cysteine pairs that crosslink heads that are not engaged, but are otherwise closely juxtaposed (J) (Chapard et al., 2019), it has been established that sister DNAs are at least some of the time entrapped between juxtaposed heads and the kleisin associated with them, namely within a J-K sub-compartment of the S-K ring (see Figure 1A for an overview of the compartments).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: BMOE-induced crosslinking of S-K rings with cysteine pairs at all three interfaces produces a covalently circular species.
source: Individual interfaces were crosslinked with efficiencies varying from 30–70% and by comparing the migration of proteins following crosslinking cysteine pairs at single (2C), double (4C), and triple (6C) interfaces, we identified a covalently circular species only produced when all three interfaces were crosslinked (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B showing the crosslinking results.

claim: Addition of 6C trimers to Scc2/Scc3/DNA mixtures produces a ladder of retarded DNA species.
source: Addition of 6C trimers to Scc2/Scc3/DNA mixtures greatly reduced the amount of DNA co-migrating with supercoiled monomers and produced a ladder of retarded DNA species, most likely caused by successive entrapment by one, two, three and more S-K rings (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D showing the DNA ladder.

claim: Ladder formation requires cysteine pairs at all three interfaces.
source: Ladder formation required cysteine pairs at all three interfaces. It was never observed with linear DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) or when just a single cysteine (Figure 1E) or BMOE (Figure 1F) was omitted.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by multiple figures showing the requirement.

claim: Ladder formation is strictly dependent on addition of ATP.
source: Crucially, the ladders were strictly dependent on addition of ATP (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1G showing ATP dependence.

claim: S-K entrapment is greatly reduced by omission of Scc2.
source: Ladders indicative of entrapment increased with time (up to 40 min), suggesting that formation is a slow process, were greatly reduced by omission of Scc2 (Figure 2A), and almost completely abolished by omission of Scc3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2A showing reduced entrapment without Scc2.

claim: S-K entrapment is almost completely abolished by omission of Scc3.
source: Ladders indicative of entrapment increased with time (up to 40 min), suggesting that formation is a slow process, were greatly reduced by omission of Scc2 (Figure 2A), and almost completely abolished by omission of Scc3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B showing abolished entrapment without Scc3.

claim: Smc3K38I mutation almost completely abolishes S-K entrapment.
source: To address the role of cohesin's ATPase, we mutated Smc3's Walker A site (Smc3K38I) to abolish ATP binding to Smc3. This almost completely abolished entrapment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2C showing the effect of the mutation.

claim: Smc1E1158Q Smc3E1155Q (EQEQ) mutations cause a modest reduction in S-K entrapment.
source: We next tested the effect of mutating both Walker B sites to residues that permit ATP binding but strongly inhibit hydrolysis (Smc1E1158Q Smc3E1155Q, 'EQEQ') (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), which caused a more modest, albeit still significant, reduction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2D showing the effect of the mutations.

claim: Smc3K112Q K113Q mutations reduce S-K entrapment.
source: To address whether Smc3's K112 K113 are also important we analysed the effect of substituting them by glutamine (Smc3K112Q K113Q), mutations thought to mimic the acetylated state. This also reduced S-K entrapment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), an effect that parallels its abrogation of cohesin loading in vivo (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing the effect of the mutations.

claim: Scc3's association with a fragment of Scc1 containing residues 269–451 greatly stimulates its association with double stranded DNA.
source: During a search for cohesin domains that bind DNA, we discovered that Scc3's association with a fragment of Scc1 containing residues 269–451 greatly stimulates its association with double stranded DNA, as measured using an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing the EMSA results.

claim: Scc3-6E mutation abolishes binding of Scc3 to DNA in the presence of Scc1.
source: In contrast, combining the two triple mutations (to create 6E) was lethal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), abolished binding of Scc3 to DNA in the presence of Scc1 (Figure 3B), and with the exception of CENs eliminated cohesin's association with the genome (Figure 3C & D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3B showing abolished DNA binding.

claim: Scc3-6E mutation is lethal.
source: In contrast, combining the two triple mutations (to create 6E) was lethal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), abolished binding of Scc3 to DNA in the presence of Scc1 (Figure 3B), and with the exception of CENs eliminated cohesin's association with the genome (Figure 3C & D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1E showing lethality.

claim: Scc3-6E mutation eliminates cohesin's association with the genome except at CENs.
source: In contrast, combining the two triple mutations (to create 6E) was lethal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), abolished binding of Scc3 to DNA in the presence of Scc1 (Figure 3B), and with the exception of CENs eliminated cohesin's association with the genome (Figure 3C & D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 3C and 3D showing ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: Cohesin containing Scc3-6E accumulated to exceptionally high levels at CENs.
source: Remarkably, cohesin containing Scc3-6E accumulated to exceptionally high levels at CENs (Figure 3C & D), which are the loading sites for most peri-centric cohesin (50 kb intervals surrounding CENs).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 3C and 3D showing ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: Cohesin containing Scc3-6E failed to support entrapment of DNAs inside S-K rings in vitro.
source: Crucially, cohesin containing Scc3-6E failed to support entrapment of DNAs inside S-K rings in vitro (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3F showing lack of entrapment.

claim: S. cerevisiae Scc2 binds DNA.
source: EMSA revealed that S. cerevisiae Scc2 also binds DNA (Figure 4A), as do Scc2/4 complexes with slightly higher affinity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4A showing EMSA results.

claim: Scc2-4E quadruple mutant greatly reduces DNA binding by Scc2.
source: In contrast, the quadruple mutant Scc2S717E K721E K788E H789E (Scc2-4E) not only greatly reduced DNA binding (Figure 4C) but also S-K entrapment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4C showing reduced DNA binding.

claim: Scc2-4E quadruple mutant reduces S-K entrapment.
source: In contrast, the quadruple mutant Scc2S717E K721E K788E H789E (Scc2-4E) not only greatly reduced DNA binding (Figure 4C) but also S-K entrapment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4D showing reduced entrapment.

claim: DNAs were never entrapped within J-S compartments.
source: However, DNAs were never entrapped within J-S compartments and only rarely by J-K ones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing lack of J-S entrapment.

claim: DNAs were only rarely entrapped within J-K compartments.
source: However, DNAs were never entrapped within J-S compartments and only rarely by J-K ones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing rare J-K entrapment.

claim: DNAs were entrapped in an ATP-dependent fashion in both E-S and E-K compartments in the presence of Scc2 and Scc3.
source: DNAs were entrapped in an ATP-dependent fashion in both E-S and E-K compartments in the presence of Scc2 and Scc3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5A showing ATP-dependent entrapment.

claim: E-S and E-K entrapment occur much more rapidly than S-K entrapment.
source: Notably, both processes occurred much more rapidly than S-K entrapment, with significant amounts of DNA entrapped by multiple rings within 2 min (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B showing rapid entrapment.

claim: The rapid entrapment of DNAs within E-S/E-K compartments in the presence of Scc2 alone was Scc3 independent.
source: In contrast to entrapment within S-K rings, which depends on Scc3, the rapid entrapment of DNA in the E-S/E-K compartments was Scc3 independent (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5C showing Scc3 independence.

claim: E-S/E-K entrapment was highly dependent on Scc2.
source: However, it was highly dependent on Scc2, both in the presence or absence of Scc3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5C showing Scc2 dependence.

claim: The rapid entrapment of DNAs within E-S/E-K compartments in the presence of Scc2 was reduced by Scc2-4E.
source: The rapid entrapment of DNAs within E-S/E-K compartments in the presence of Scc2 was reduced by Scc2-4E (Figure 5E), suggesting that the reaction at least partly depends on Scc2's ability to bind DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5E showing reduced entrapment with Scc2-4E.

claim: E-S/E-K entrapment was unaffected by Smc1E1158Q Smc3E1155Q mutations (EQEQ).
source: Strikingly, both types of entrapment were unaffected by Smc1E1158Q Smc3E1155Q mutations (EQEQ), implying that neither form of entrapment requires ATP hydrolysis (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5F showing no effect of EQEQ mutations.

claim: E-S entrapment in the presence of Scc2 alone was only modestly reduced by Smc3K38I.
source: In contrast to S-K entrapment in the presence of both Scc2 and Scc3 (Figure 2C), E-S entrapment in the presence of Scc2 alone was only modestly reduced by Smc3K38I, implying that ATP bound merely to Smc1's ATPase head is sufficient (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5G showing modest reduction with Smc3K38I.

claim: In the presence of Scc2 alone, few if any DNAs are entrapped in S-K compartments by 2 min.
source: In contrast with E-S or E-K entrapment, which is very efficient, few if any DNAs are entrapped in S-K compartments by 2 min (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5H showing lack of S-K entrapment at 2 min.

claim: Double crosslinking of hinge and coiled coils occurs efficiently in the presence of ATP.
source: As expected, double crosslinking also occurred efficiently when the coiled coil pair was combined with one within the hinge interface (Smc1K639C Smc3E570C). These cysteine pair combinations enabled us to measure entrapment within two sub-compartments within the E-S compartment (Figure 6A iii): one created by simultaneous crosslinking of the hinge and coiled coils (C-H compartment) (Figure 6A ii) and a complementary one made by the simultaneous crosslinking of coiled coils and engaged heads (E-C compartment) (Figure 6A i).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6B showing efficient crosslinking.

claim: Few if any DNAs were entrapped in the C-H sub-compartment in the presence of Scc2 and ATP.
source: Despite efficient crosslinking at both cysteine pairs (Figure 6B), few if any DNAs were entrapped in the presence of Scc2 and ATP following BMOE treatment of cohesin trimers containing hinge and coiled coil cysteine pairs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6C showing lack of C-H entrapment.

claim: Few if any DNAs were entrapped in the E-C sub-compartment.
source: Likewise, few if any DNAs were entrapped by cohesin trimers containing both E-state and coiled coil cysteine pairs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Entrapment of DNAs within E-S compartments in the presence of Scc2 is accompanied by dissociation of their coiled coils.
source: We deduce from this result that entrapment of DNAs within E-S compartments in the presence of Scc2 is accompanied by dissociation of their coiled coils in a manner that precludes crosslinking between Smc1K201C and Smc3K198C.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a deduction from the experimental results.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of EQEQ cohesin trimers bound to ATP, linear DNA, and Scc2C2 was solved to a resolution of 3.4 Å.
source: To elucidate how DNA actually associates with EQEQ cohesin trimers in the presence of ATP and Scc2, but lacking Scc3, namely under conditions in which DNAs are clearly entrapped within E-S and E-K but not S-K compartments, we used cryo-EM to solve the structure of EQEQ cohesin trimers (Smc1, Smc3 and Scc1) bound to ATP, linear DNA (40 bp), and Scc2C2 (residues 151–1493) to a resolution of 3.4 Å (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7A showing the cryo-EM map.

claim: The structure associated with circular DNA is virtually identical to that associated with the linear oligonucleotide.
source: Crucially, the structure associated with circular DNA is virtually identical to that associated with the linear oligonucleotide and since the former is known to involve E-S/E-K but not S-K entrapment, we can with some certainty infer the path of the kleisin chain with respect to the DNA (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8F showing the kleisin path.

claim: E-S/E-K entrapment arises from the clamping of DNA between Scc2 and engaged heads.
source: First and foremost, E-S/E-K entrapment does indeed arise from the clamping of DNA between Scc2 and engaged heads in the manner revealed by both high (Figure 7A) and medium (Figure 7B) resolution cryo-EM structures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 7A and 7B showing the clamped state.

claim: The DNA must have entered the clamped state without formation of a loop.
source: Second, because the circular DNA is demonstrably not highly-bent when clamped (Figure 7B, right), the DNA must have entered the clamped state and thereby been entrapped in E-S/E-K compartments without formation of a loop (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7B showing unbent circular DNA.

claim: A single segment of DNA must have been passed between the heads prior to their engagement.
source: In other words, a single segment of DNA must have been passed between the heads prior to their engagement (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Binding of DNA by Scc2 in S. cerevisiae cohesin occurs in a similar manner to that described for human Scc2NIPBL.
source: Binding of DNA by Scc2 in S. cerevisiae cohesin occurs in a similar manner to that recently described for human Scc2NIPBL (Shi et al., 2020; Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation and supported by Figure 8A.

claim: Scc2 holds DNA by way of a curved basic and polar surface located around the transition between its neck and head regions.
source: Scc2 holds DNA by way of a curved basic and polar surface located around the transition between its neck and head regions (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8B showing the DNA binding surface.

claim: Scc2 binds to Smc1 through HEAT repeats 18–24 that dock onto the F-loop on Smc1 and the emerging coiled coils above it.
source: Highly prominent is the binding of Scc2 to Smc1 through the docking of HEAT repeats 18–24 (residues 1127–1493) onto the F-loop (residues 1095–1118) on Smc1 head's C-lobe and the coiled coils that emerge above (Figure 8C i).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8C i showing the binding interface.

claim: Scc2 interacts with Smc3's N-lobe through a β-strand that docks onto the end of the central β-sheet of the Smc3 head.
source: One key contact in this regard involves residues in an otherwise disordered loop (1178–1203) that form a β-strand which docks onto the end of the central β-sheet of the Smc3 head (Figure 8C iii).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8C iii showing the binding interface.

claim: Salt bridges form between aspartate and glutamate residues in Scc2 loops and Smc3 K112 K113.
source: More conserved is a major contact mediated by salt bridges between a collection of highly conserved aspartate and glutamate residues located within two loops of Scc2 (819-EDEED-823 and 781-DD-782) and two key lysine residues (K112 K113) in Smc3 (Figure 8C ii).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8C ii showing the salt bridges.

claim: The engaged heads of Smc1 and Smc3 produce a 2-fold pseudo-symmetrical ABC ATPase heterodimer that binds DNA through two sites exactly two turns of the DNA apart.
source: While Scc2 holds the upper half of the DNA's backbone through a spiral of basic and polar residues (Figure 8B), the engaged heads of Smc1 and Smc3 produce a 2-fold pseudo-symmetrical ABC ATPase heterodimer that binds DNA through two sites that are exactly two turns of the DNA apart and coincide with the major groove in the DNA (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8D showing the pseudo-symmetrical binding.

claim: Smc3 K112 and K113 face towards the two aspartate and glutamate rich loops in Scc2.
source: However, close inspection of their side chains shows that they in fact face towards the two aspartate and glutamate rich loops in Scc2 (819-EDEED-823 and 781-DD-782) (Figure 8C ii), implying that they engage in ionic interactions between Smc3 and Scc2 as well as or instead of DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8C ii showing the orientation of K112 K113.

claim: Scc1's two structured domains are bound in a canonical manner to Smc3's neck and the base of Smc1's ATPase.
source: Though our map (Figure 7A) shows little to no density for residues of Scc1 known to bind the central cleft of Scc2 (Scc1 residues ~ 190–290), it shows very clearly that Scc1's two structured domains,Scc1-N (residues 67–103) and Scc1-C (residues 502–555), are bound in a canonical manner to Smc3's neck and the base of Smc1's ATPase respectively (Gligoris et al., 2014; Haering et al., 2004) thereby bridging the two heads to form the S-K ring (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations and supported by Figure 8F.

claim: Addition of Scc2 and DNA in the absence of ATP caused a ~50% reduction in J-state crosslinking.
source: Surprisingly, addition of Scc2 and DNA in the absence of ATP had the greatest effect, causing a ~ 50% reduction in J crosslinking, an effect that was highly reproducible.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a finding from the experiments.

claim: In the absence of ATP, both Scc2 and DNA reduce J-specific crosslinking by driving or holding the ATPase heads apart.
source: We therefore suggest that in the absence of ATP, both Scc2 and DNA reduce J-specific crosslinking by driving or indeed holding the ATPase heads apart, a process that could facilitate passage of DNA between them and thereby facilitate its entrapment in E-S compartments when heads engage in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a suggestion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The in vitro S-K entrapment activity involves mechanisms similar or identical to those of cohesin operating within cells.
source: We therefore suggest that the in vitro DNA S-K entrapment described here involves mechanisms similar or identical to those of cohesin operating within cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the properties of the in vitro system.

claim: E-S/E-K entrapment is an order of magnitude more rapid than S-K entrapment.
source: Because E-S/E-K entrapment is an order of magnitude more rapid than S-K entrapment, we suggest that creation of the former by Scc2 may be a precursor to the latter, a process contingent on the action of Scc3.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the kinetic differences.

claim: Creation of E-S/E-K entrapment by Scc2 may be a precursor to S-K entrapment.
source: Because E-S/E-K entrapment is an order of magnitude more rapid than S-K entrapment, we suggest that creation of the former by Scc2 may be a precursor to the latter, a process contingent on the action of Scc3.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the kinetic differences.

claim: The clamping of DNAs between Scc2NIPBL and engaged heads may be a key intermediate during the process of S-K entrapment.
source: In other words, the clamping of DNAs between Scc2NIPBL and engaged heads may be a key intermediate during the process of S-K entrapment and hence crucial for the establishment of sister chromatid cohesion.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the findings.

claim: The clamping of DNA between Scc2NIPBL and engaged heads followed by release upon ATP hydrolysis may be the driving force for cohesin's translocation along DNA.
source: The clamping of DNA between Scc2NIPBL and engaged heads and subsequent release upon ATP hydrolysis, all in the absence of S-K entrapment, may be the driving force for cohesin's translocation along DNA, a notion fully consistent with Scc2's key role in stimulating DNA-dependent ATP hydrolysis (Petela et al., 2018) and loop extrusion (Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion with citations to support the role of Scc2.

claim: Scc3 has a unique role in promoting entry of DNA inside the SMC-kleisin ring.
source: Our finding that Scc3 is essential for S-K but not E-S/E-K entrapment reveals that Scc3 has a unique role in promoting entry of DNA inside the SMC-kleisin ring as well as being necessary for loop extrusion (Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a finding with a citation to support the role in loop extrusion.

claim: S-K entrapment in vivo is not abolished by fusing Scc1's NTD to Smc3 or by fusing its CTD to Smc1.
source: Crucially, S-K entrapment in vivo is not abolished by fusing Scc1's NTD to Smc3 or by fusing its CTD to Smc1, implying that DNA must enter either through the hinge or through dissociation of either one of the two SMC-kleisin interfaces (possibly through simultaneous dissociation of both) (Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Folding of cohesin's coiled coils around an elbow brings its hinge domain into close proximity to DNA bound to the heads.
source: Nevertheless, hinge opening is equally plausible, especially in the light of recent findings that folding of cohesin's coiled coils around an elbow brings its hinge domain into close proximity to DNA bound to the heads, and that Scc3SA2 interacts with a half opened hinge when DNA is bound to human cohesin-Scc2NIPBL complexes (Bürmann et al., 2019; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the structural findings.

claim: Scc3's ability to bind DNA depends on two sets of residues (K224 K225 R226 and K423 K513 K520).
source: This feature of Scc3's activity depends on its ability to bind DNA in a manner similar to that employed by Scc2 (this work) (Li et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020) and condensin's Ycg1 HAWK (Kschonsak et al., 2017). Two sets of residues are implicated in DNA binding (K224 K225 R226 and K423 K513 K520).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the DNA binding mechanism.

claim: Mutation of both sets of DNA binding residues in Scc3 (Scc3-6E) abolishes DNA binding and is lethal.
source: Mutation of one or other set does not abrogate DNA binding or cause lethality but does reduce cohesin's association with chromosomes while mutation of both sets (Scc3-6E) abolishes not only DNA binding and S-K entrapment in vitro but is lethal and abolishes all loading throughout the genome in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Scc3-6E has no effect on Scc2 driven E-S/E-K entrapment.
source: Though it abrogates entrapment of DNA within S-K compartments (Figure 3F), Scc3-6E has no effect on Scc2 driven E-S/E-K entrapment (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Complete depletion of Scc3 abrogates cohesin's association at CENs as well as along chromosomes arms.
source: Unlike Scc3-6E, complete depletion of Scc3 abrogates cohesin's association at CENs as well as along chromosomes arms, which implies that Scc3 has additional functions that do not involve or require its ability to bind DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a finding from the experiments.
